title: Coherent localization comparison for exact inverse image
statement:
Let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a geometric morphism between sheaf topoi on small sites, meaning an adjunction $f^{-1}\dashv f_*$ whose inverse image preserves finite limits [def-weil-pbc-sites-and-cohomology]. Let $R$ be a sheaf of commutative rings on $\mathcal Y$ and let $t$ be a global section. Put $R'=f^{-1}R$ and $t'=f^{-1}t$. Module sheaves, sheafified localization and ordinary unbounded derived categories are as in [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category, def-weil-pbc-ringed-section-localization, def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. On modules set $M[1/t]=R[1/t]\otimes_R M$, using the sheaf tensor product [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product]. There are canonical ring and module isomorphisms
$$f^{-1}(R[1/t])\cong R'[1/t'],\qquad \beta_{f,M}:f^{-1}(M[1/t])\xrightarrow{\sim}(f^{-1}M)[1/t'].$$
They preserve the localization units and on local fraction representatives send $m/t^n$ to the inverse-image representative of $m$ divided by $(t')^n$. Both module inverse image with these identified rings and scalar localization are exact. Their termwise derived functors therefore have the same natural comparison $\beta_f$, with no bound on the complex. For another geometric morphism $g:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$, the comparison for $f\circ g$ is the composite of $g^{-1}\beta_f$ and $\beta_g$ after inserting the canonical inverse-image composition isomorphisms on source and target; the identity comparison is the identity under the canonical identity inverse image. These are equations of natural transformations, including their derived versions. The comparison also commutes with a specified identification $f^{-1}R\cong S$ by a ring-sheaf isomorphism and the induced identification of the scalar sections.

proof.text: Use the declared localization-away sequential-colimit theorem for the regular module. The usual algebra equivalence from localization of the regular module to the away-localized ring identifies its stage-n leg with r/t^n. Evaluation and the presheaf-module colimit theorem make this a colimit of presheaf modules. Tensor on the left by the given module presheaf, using its right-unitor identification on the diagram. This gives the colimit with vertex M tensor P_t(R). Module sheafification preserves it. Its vertex is isomorphic to the actual site tensor M tensor P_t(R)^#: the sheafification unit of P_t(R) is a local equivalence, tensoring preserves local equivalences, and sheafification inverts them. Naturality of the sheafification unit proves that stage zero is exactly the specified map m to m tensor 1.

proof.text:
The ring localization has the following mapping property directly from its construction. For a map of commutative ring sheaves $a:A\to B$ for which $a(s)$ is invertible, the ordinary localization property defines on every object $U$ the unique map
$$P_s(A)(U)\to B(U),\qquad r/s_U^n\longmapsto a_U(r)a(s)_U^{-n}.$$
Uniqueness makes these maps compatible with restrictions, and ring sheafification extends them uniquely to $A[1/s]\to B$. Conversely any such extension takes $1/s$ to the inverse of $a(s)$. Consequently restriction along $A\to A[1/s]$ is a bijection onto the maps that invert $s$. This also proves uniqueness over $A$, even for the zero ring or a nilpotent $s$.

proof.text: In any colimit of the repeated scalar endomorphism, multiplication by the scalar is invertible: the map induced by shifting the legs one place is its inverse. For a module sheaf N with invertible scalar, two maps from this colimit agreeing at stage zero agree at every stage, by induction, scalar-linearity, the cocone relation and cancellation of the target scalar. Thus the stage-zero unit determines a map uniquely. Apply this to the tensor-localization colimit from step 1.

proof.text: Transport any morphism of source ring sheaves through the specified underlying-set isomorphisms. Its additive and multiplicative compatibility follows by choosing a preimage of a pair under the invertible finite-product comparison and applying the two ring graph equations. The one graph equation gives preservation of one. Apply this construction to R to R[1/t], obtaining c:S to A. The source inverse of t is a compatible family by uniqueness of inverses; the ring graph equations and the assumed scalar normalization show c(s) is invertible. Step 2 produces a ring map S[1/s] to A extending c. The regular-module colimit from step 1, after forgetting to set sheaves and applying the proved ring/module localization comparison, is the underlying set-sheaf colimit for the ring localization. The set inverse image preserves it. Transport its diagram by the ring underlying isomorphism and the scalar graph equation. This is a second colimit of the S-multiplication-by-s diagram, now with vertex the underlying set sheaf of A and zero leg c. The extension map respects every leg: the zero case is its unit equation, and the successor case follows by multiplication with the invertible c(s), the cocone relations, and multiplicativity. Consequently its underlying map is the unique isomorphism between the two colimits. The forgetful functor reflects isomorphisms, so it is a ring isomorphism. Invert it for the displayed comparison. Step 2 gives uniqueness from the same unit equation.

proof.text: The module-to-abelian-sheaf functor preserves colimits by the declared forgetful-colimit theorem. Forgetting abelian sheaves to set sheaves preserves sequential filtered colimits: the abelian-group forgetful functor preserves filtered colimits and commutes with sheafification. Hence the module-underlying-set functor preserves these colimits. The underlying-set isomorphism for the specified module inverse image and preservation of colimits by the set left adjoint imply preservation of sequential colimits by the module inverse image, since the target underlying functor reflects them. The module scalar graph and the section normalization identify the image diagram with the repeated target-scalar diagram. The unique isomorphism between this colimit and the tensor-localization colimit gives beta. Stage zero proves unit normalization; the uniqueness lemma of step 3 proves naturality in M and uniqueness of beta.

proof.text: Naturality of the comparisons is obtained as in step 5. For the generalized fraction formula, form the natural map from any test sheaf to the ring with constant value t^n on each object. Induction using ringOne and ringMul identifies its inverse image with the constant value (t′)^n; the hypothesis identifying the inverse-image section gives the induction step. Apply the moduleSMul graph equation to the given equality t^n q = eta(m). Naturality of moduleUnderlying transports the unit map, and the assumed unit-normalization equation for beta changes the result to the target localization unit. Componentwise linearity of beta gives the required equation. Exponent zero follows from ringOne. This uses generalized sections and no points.

proof.text: Convert the given algebraic inverse-image presentation to the independent-universe presentation by the explicit ULift/down isomorphisms on set sheaves. Transport every ring and module graph equation across these isomorphisms. Apply geometric_inverse_image_exact to the geometric morphism made from the specified adjunction and finite-limit preservation. This proves the inverse-image part of localization_inverseImage_exact without reconstructing its module adjunction.

proof.text: For scalar localization, the presheaf of localized coefficients is sectionwise flat by IsLocalization.flat. Hence sectionwise tensoring with it preserves finite limits; evaluation jointly reflects presheaf-module limits. The module-sheafification adjunction is left exact, and monoidal sheafification together with its invertible counit identifies tensoring the sheafified localization with forgetting, tensoring the presheaf localization, and sheafifying. Thus tensoring the sheafified localization preserves finite limits. The explicit site tensor agrees with this monoidal tensor by siteSheafTensorRightIso. The cochain tensor API gives finite-colimit preservation and additivity of this tensor, and the isomorphism transports these properties to scalarLocalization. Apply the argument on both sites.

For $g:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$, put $J=g^{-1}$ and $R''=J(R')$, with section $t''=J(t')$. The inverse image of $f\circ g$ is canonically identified with $JI$ by the composite adjunction and its unit-preserving uniqueness isomorphism. The comparison transports ring and module operations: by naturality it commutes with each operation map, and compatibility with finite-product comparisons follows by checking the projections. Its naturality at the localization-unit maps identifies the composite inverse image of those maps with their iterated inverse image. Under these source and coefficient identifications both
$$\beta_{f\circ g,M}\quad\hbox{and}\quad\beta_{g,IM}\circ J(\beta_{f,M})$$
are $R''$-linear maps $JI(M[1/t])\to(JIM)[1/t'']$ which, after precomposition with $JI(\eta_M)$, equal $\eta_{JIM}$: for the second map, first use $\beta_f I(\eta_M)=\eta_{IM}$, then $\beta_g J(\eta_{IM})=\eta_{JIM}$. Applying the initial property in step 5 successively to $I$ and $J$ gives uniqueness for this source; hence the two maps are equal. The ring comparisons agree by exactly the ring extension uniqueness of step 4, since both restrict to the identity of $R''$. For the identity adjunction, the identity map extends the localization unit, so the same uniqueness gives the identity comparison. These are equalities on every module and are natural by step 6, hence equations of natural transformations with the canonical composition and identity isomorphisms inserted.

source.place: Adjunction composition and uniqueness; agent normalization calculation using the unit characterizations proved in steps 4--5

proof.text: For a specified ring-sheaf isomorphism $c:R'\xrightarrow{\sim}S$, let $u=c(t')$. Step 2 extends $c$ uniquely to $c_{\mathrm{loc}}:R'[1/t']\to S[1/u]$, by $r/(t')^n\mapsto c(r)/u^n$; extending $c^{-1}$ gives its inverse. Reinterpret any $R'$-module as an $S$-module using $c^{-1}$. Under this equivalence, $t'$-invertibility is precisely $u$-invertibility and the localization units are the same maps. Thus step 3 identifies the two module localizations uniquely, compatibly with $c_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The comparison obtained from $\beta_f$ using these identifications and the comparison constructed with the identified ring $S$ both extend $I(\eta_M)$ to the same unit; uniqueness in step 5 proves the required commuting square. The explicit fraction formulas also show preservation of the specified scalar section. Coefficient reinterpretation leaves the underlying abelian sheaves and their kernels and cokernels unchanged, so it is exact.

source.place: Tag 00CP, uniqueness and formula for localization lifts; module extension formulas of step 3

proof.text: Apply the exact-functor derived factorization to inverse image and scalar localization, using steps 7--8. They preserve quasi-isomorphisms and act on every unbounded cochain complex termwise; the exact-functor derived-functor theorem identifies these functors with their left and right derived functors. Naturality of $\beta_f$ makes its degreewise components a chain isomorphism, since the square for every differential is its module naturality square. The localization universal property for natural transformations descends it to an isomorphism on the unbounded derived categories. It also descends the natural comparisons for exact coefficient reinterpretation and for identity and composition. The equations of steps 9--10 hold degreewise on all complexes; the faithfulness assertion for precomposition with the derived localization makes the descended equations equalities of natural transformations. Thus the specified coherence persists on the full ordinary derived categories, with no boundedness hypothesis or choice of resolution. For the derived unit equation, define privately the localization lift of an arbitrary natural transformation, prove its factorization equation on complexes, and use localization extensionality to prove naturality of the derived composition comparison under left and right whiskering. Apply these two equations to the original unit-normalization equation and cancel the identity/composition comparison isomorphisms. For localized-scalar full faithfulness, extend an original-ring-linear map objectwise across the ordinary localization by LinearMap.extendScalarsOfIsLocalization. The localization ring sheafification unit is locally surjective, as follows from its module sheafification comparison. Descend the pointwise extended map with restrictHomEquivOfIsLocallySurjective. Componentwise equality proves both its restriction equation and uniqueness.
